name: Varsen RadSeal Contamination Suit Mk-IV
description:
A full-body radiation containment suit in dull ochre with charcoal seam tape, constructed from trilaminate lead-weave bonded to a breathable rad-absorb membrane. Shelf workers near the old reactor spillways wear these until the seams crack and the hood seal whistles. Pre-owned units show yellowing at the chest bib and scorch rings around the boot cuffs.

The hood integrates a replaceable carbon-filter cartridge and a polycarbonate face shield scratched from years of particulate exposure. Wrist and ankle closures use double-roll gasketing. Seams are RF-welded, not stitched.
functionality: Rated for low-to-mid ionizing radiation exposure up to 8-hour shift duration; replaceable hood filter cartridges extend usable life; double-roll gasket closures at wrists, ankles, and hood neck ring prevent particulate ingress; boot soles are acid-resistant nitrile.
what_it_says: You work somewhere that will kill you slowly, and you know it.
story_hooks: A suit returned to a Shelf secondhand stall still has a name written in marker inside the hood — and that person was reported dead six months ago.
A Tier 2 maintenance tech discovers their RadSeal Mk-IV is three certification cycles out of date — their supervisor has been falsifying inspection records.
The carbon filter cartridges have been counterfeited; a runner needs to trace the supply chain before the next shift rotation kills a dozen workers.

physical_description.visual_profile: A utilitarian full-body silhouette with pronounced shoulders and a bulky torso. The hood dominates the upper half, creating an almost avian profile. Visually reads as industrial hazmat wear—functional and intimidating rather than fashionable.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and deliberate—cut to layer over base garments without restriction. The proportions are generous through the torso and thighs, tapering slightly at wrists and ankles for gasketed seals. Intentionally not form-fitting.
physical_description.primary_material: Trilaminate lead-weave outer shell bonded to a breathable rad-absorb membrane. RF-welded seams throughout. Polycarbonate face shield integrated into hood. Carbon-filter cartridge housing.
physical_description.texture: Dull, matte finish with a subtle woven grid visible in raking light. Charcoal seam tape creates tactile ribs running vertically and horizontally across the body. Areas showing wear appear slightly tacky from degraded membrane. Face shield is scratched and frosted in patches.
physical_description.color_scheme: Dull ochre primary with charcoal grey seam tape and RF-weld lines. Yellowing patches across chest bib and upper shoulders indicate age and exposure. Scorched rings (dark brown-black) around boot cuffs from thermal exposure.
physical_description.closures: Double-roll gasketing at wrists and ankles—designed for airtight sealing. Hood likely uses a friction-fit gasket seal at the neck. No visible buckles or zippers; the suit is a pull-over design.
distinctive_features: Integrated polycarbonate face shield scratched and clouded from years of particulate exposure
Replaceable carbon-filter cartridge housing at mouth level
Pronounced bib panel on chest—primary contamination contact zone
RF-welded seams instead of stitching—visible as raised charcoal tape lines
Double-roll gasket cuffs at wrists and ankles
Yellowing and discoloration indicating age and accumulated radiation dose
Scorch rings around boot cuffs from thermal events
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 4-5 functional/salvage. Varsen Industrial Safety is mid-market safety equipment; these suits are affordable for working-class hazmat labor but often sold second or third-hand. A pre-owned unit signals economic necessity.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by reactor spillway shelf workers, contamination zone laborers, and sub-grade salvagers. Signals exposure to industrial hazards, low-wage labor, and proximity to the GLMZ's decaying infrastructure. Also worn by hobbyist radiophiles and anti-corpo protest movements as anti-establishment fashion.
physical_description.condition_typical: Visibly aged and worn. Seams crack and split after 200-400 hours of use. The hood seal develops a characteristic whistle as gasket material degrades. Pre-owned units show yellowing, scorch marks, and clouded face shields. Most street units are 5-12 years past their rated service life.
